Wireless Mic Rentals

Why we quote the microphone and the speakers together.

Most people searching for a microphone rental need a speaker and microphone rental: a working sound system. A microphone does not make anyone louder on its own. What makes the back row hear the toast, the vows or the keynote is the speaker, the mixer, the gain structure and the person who set all three.

So every microphone goes out as part of a complete system: speakers sized to your room and headcount, a mixer, stands, cabling and power, tuned on-site by our technician before anyone walks in. That is why a single wireless handheld from us sounds different from the same model out of a box.

If you already know you need a bigger PA (a ballroom, an outdoor ceremony, a live band), start with the full sound system page and we will fold the microphones into the same quote.

What We Carry

Every kind of wireless microphone rental a Dallas-Fort Worth event asks for.

Tell us who is speaking and how they need to move, and we will bring the right one. Most events end up with a mix: a handheld for the room, a lapel for the person on stage, and something on the podium that nobody has to think about.

Type One

Wireless handheld microphone rental

Digital wireless handhelds that get passed between speakers, handed to a best man, walked into an audience for questions or carried by an emcee for four hours without a dropout. This is the microphone most events use most of the night.

We bring spares, we bring fresh batteries, and we swap them mid-event before anyone notices a level moving.

Best for Toasts, emcees, keynotes, auctions, Q&A, awards, anything that gets passed hand to hand.
Type Two

Lapel & lavalier microphone rental

Clip-on lavalier microphones on wireless bodypacks, for the presenter who needs both hands and does not want a microphone in the photographs. This is the standard for officiants, panelists and anyone being recorded.

We place them ourselves. Lapel microphones usually fail because of where they get clipped, and that is a two-minute fix nobody performs when the gear is dropped off.

Best for Officiants, panel discussions, interviews, podcasts, video shoots, worship services.
Type Three

Headset microphone rental

Over-the-ear headset microphones that keep a consistent distance from the mouth no matter how much the speaker turns, gestures or walks. An hour in, the presenter still sounds the same.

Because the capsule stays put, headsets hold gain better than a handheld or a lapel, which matters in a loud or reverberant room.

Best for Trainers, fitness and dance instructors, worship leaders, long-form presenters, stage performers.
Type Four

Podium & lectern microphone rental

A gooseneck microphone mounted to the lectern, or a stand-mounted podium microphone where there is no lectern to mount to. Set once, aimed properly, and it works for everyone who steps up to it.

This is the setup that goes wrong most often at hotels and venues: a podium microphone aimed at a chest instead of a mouth, feeding back the moment the room fills. We aim it and set it with a person standing there, and because De-Feedback comes with every microphone we send out, there is no ringing out involved and no feedback once the room fills.

Best for Award ceremonies, graduations, conferences, city and council meetings, memorials, press events.
Type Five

Conference & board room microphones

Push-to-talk tabletop microphones: one per seat, live only while the button is held. That keeps a table full of open microphones from picking up the same shuffling papers, side conversations and air handling, and it means the person speaking is clearly the person you hear.

It also gives you a clean feed for the recording or the stream, because only the person talking is ever open.

Best for Board meetings, council chambers, committee hearings, depositions, meeting rooms, hybrid conference rooms.
Type Six

Instrument, choir & stage microphones

Drum kits, guitar cabinets, acoustic instruments, choir and overhead coverage, plus the stands, clips and cabling that go with them. Once a band is playing you are not picking microphones any more, you are building an input list.

Send us the stage plot or the input list and we will bring what it calls for, along with monitoring so the players can hear themselves.

Best for Live bands, worship teams, school and university performances, recitals, recorded sets.

Not sure which one you need?

That is the normal starting point, and sorting it out is part of the job. Describe the room, the headcount and who is speaking, and we will come back with the specific microphone complement for it, including the ones you had not thought to ask for, like a spare handheld for floor questions or a second lapel on the person being interviewed.

De-Feedback

Every open microphone is one step from feedback.

It shows up at the worst moment: the officiant leaning in, the award winner turning to hug someone, the panelist gesturing with the handheld, the speaker stepping in front of the speakers.

Our AI-powered De-Feedback system runs on every microphone we rent, at no extra line item. It listens for the ring before it becomes a squeal and takes that frequency out, which means your speakers can move the way people naturally move instead of being coached to stand on a piece of tape.

It matters more than it used to. Rooms with a stream or a recording run hotter, because the same microphones feed the PA and the broadcast, and that is the condition that makes an untreated system ring. This is also why we would rather set the microphone up ourselves than hand it over: the suppression is running on our system, tuned for your room.

The clip beside this walks through what the system is watching for. The waveform runs clean, one frequency finds the loop and rings up, the level meter climbs into the red, and then the suppression takes that frequency out and the voice keeps all of its tone.

Which Microphone, Which Room

What we would bring for your room, based on what you are running.

These are the setups we build most often across the Metroplex. Yours will differ in some detail, but this is the shape of the answer.

Wedding ceremonyOutdoor or garden

Rig 1 lapel · 1 handheld · compact system

A lapel microphone on the officiant and a discreet handheld or second lavalier for the couple’s vows, run into a compact system placed where it covers the seats without appearing in a single photograph. Wind is the real enemy outdoors, so the capsules get proper screening and we set levels with someone standing at the altar, not at the mixer. See wedding audio.

Reception & toastsBallroom or venue hall

Rig 2 wireless handhelds · reception system

Two wireless handhelds so one is always charged and in someone’s hand, plus the reception system doing double duty for music. Toasts are the riskiest microphone moment at a wedding: people who have never held one, holding it at their chest, in a room full of conversation. That is what the feedback suppression and a technician riding the level are for.

Conference keynoteHotel ballroom or general session

Rig 1 headset or lapel · 1 podium · 2 handhelds on stands

A headset or lapel on the presenter, a podium microphone for introductions and a pair of handhelds on stands for floor questions, all mixed into a system that covers front-to-back evenly rather than blasting row one to reach row twenty. Add a confidence feed and the microphones for panels that follow. See corporate AV.

Panel discussionStage or head table

Rig 1 mic per panelist · moderator mic · 1 roaming handheld

One microphone per panelist (lapels if they are on stools or standing, tabletop push-to-talk if they are seated at a table), plus a moderator microphone and at least one roaming handheld for the audience. Sharing microphones across a panel is a common reason a recorded panel is unusable afterwards.

Board & committee meetingBoard room or council chamber

Rig push-to-talk tabletop, one per seat · clean feed out

Push-to-talk tabletop microphones, one per seat, so the minutes are clean and the remote attendees hear a person instead of a room. We set the coverage so nobody has to lean, and we can send a clean feed straight into whatever platform the meeting is on. Pairs naturally with live streaming.

Worship serviceSanctuary or multipurpose room

Rig 1 headset · handhelds · podium · choir and instrument coverage

A headset on the pastor, handhelds and a podium microphone for readings and announcements, and instrument or choir coverage for the music team. Sanctuaries are hard rooms: hard surfaces, high ceilings, microphones a long way in front of the speakers. That is where the feedback suppression matters most.

Press conferencePodium or step-and-repeat

Rig 1 podium mic · press feed · handhelds for questions

A podium microphone plus a press feed so every outlet in the room pulls clean audio from the same source instead of stacking a dozen recorders on the lectern. Handhelds for questions from the floor, so the answer makes sense on the recording.

Live band or ensembleVenue, campus or outdoor stage

Rig full input list · stage monitoring

A full input list covering drums, amps, acoustic instruments and vocals, with monitoring so the band can hear themselves, mixed by someone who has done it before. Send the stage plot and we will build to it. See live music events.

How It Works

From your first message to the microphone being live.

We do every step below ourselves, including the ones that happen while your guests are in the room.

Date, venue, roughly how many people and who is speaking. That is enough for us to know what the microphone complement should be.

We spec it

Questions

What people ask before they book microphones.

Can I rent just a microphone on its own?
We quote it as a speaker and microphone rental, because microphones go out as part of a full sound system. A microphone does not make anyone louder by itself: the speaker, the mixer and the setup do that. Bundling them is also what lets us guarantee it works when the room fills, because we tuned the whole chain together. More on sound system rental.
What kinds of microphones do you carry?
Wireless handhelds, lapel and lavalier microphones on bodypacks, over-the-ear headsets, gooseneck podium and lectern microphones, push-to-talk tabletop microphones for conference and board rooms, and instrument, choir and overhead microphones for bands and worship teams. Most events use a combination, and working out that combination is part of the quote.
What is the AI De-Feedback system?
It is feedback suppression that runs on every microphone we rent, standard. It identifies the frequency that is about to ring and removes it before the room hears a squeal, which lets speakers move naturally instead of being told to stay behind a line. It is running on our system, tuned for your room, which is one of the reasons we set the microphones up ourselves.
Do you deliver and set up, or do I pick the equipment up?
We deliver, build, line-check, run and strike everything ourselves. A technician is on-site for the event as part of the rental, which is how we can stand behind the way it sounds once the room fills.
How many microphones do I need for a panel?
One per panelist, plus a moderator microphone and at least one roaming handheld for audience questions. Panelists sharing a microphone is a common reason a recorded panel turns out unusable, and it slows the discussion down in the room as well.
Do you have microphones for a podium or lectern?
Yes. Gooseneck microphones that mount to a lectern, and stand-mounted podium microphones where there is nothing to mount to. We aim it and set it with someone standing at it, which is the step most podium setups skip. Every microphone we send out includes the De-Feedback system, so there is no ringing out involved and the podium holds up once the room fills.
Can everyone at the board table have their own microphone?
Yes. For board meetings, council sessions, committee hearings and hybrid meeting rooms we set push-to-talk tabletop microphones, one per seat, live only while the button is held. That keeps a table of open microphones from picking up shuffling papers and side conversations, and it gives you a clean feed for the recording or the stream.
Do you have lapel and headset microphones?
Both, on wireless bodypacks. Lapel and lavalier microphones are the standard for officiants, panelists and anyone being filmed; headsets hold a consistent distance from the mouth and hold gain better, which makes them the right answer for long presentations, instructors and worship leaders. We place them on the person rather than handing them over in a bag.
Will a wireless microphone work outdoors?
Yes, and outdoor ceremonies are a large share of what we do. Outdoors the issues are wind and coverage rather than feedback, so capsules get proper screening and the system is placed to cover the seating area rather than the open field behind it. We also bring power solutions for sites without a convenient outlet.
What areas of Dallas-Fort Worth do you serve?
The whole Metroplex: roughly a forty-mile radius from the mid-cities, covering Dallas, Fort Worth, Arlington, Plano, Frisco, Irving, Southlake, McKinney, Richardson, Grapevine, Denton and everywhere in between. If your venue is further out, ask anyway and we will tell you honestly whether it works.

Tell us who is speaking. We’ll bring the right microphone.
